subcategory: Stable Average Float Masking a Critical Path Shift
skill: Recognizing that unchanged schedule-wide average float can mask a genuine forecast slip caused by a critical path shift
scenario: An airport terminal expansion project tracks 'average Total Float across all remaining activities' as a headline schedule health KPI. This average has remained almost unchanged, 14.2 days last month versus 14.6 days this month. In the same period, the CPM forecast finish slipped by six weeks, because the baggage handling system integration path - previously carrying 60+ days of float - lost nearly all of it, while a separate utility tie-in path, previously near-critical, gained substantial float after an early completion.
question: How can a schedule-wide average float statistic stay essentially flat while the forecast finish slips by six weeks? What does this reveal about using average float as a health KPI?
expectedAnswer: Average float is a summary statistic across all activities and paths; it can remain stable even while individual paths move sharply in opposite directions, as long as the gains and losses roughly offset in the aggregate. Here, the baggage handling path's float collapse (say, from 65 days to 4 days) and the utility tie-in path's float gain (say, from 8 days to 45 days after early completion freed up capacity) can average out to almost no net change, even though the baggage handling path becoming the new near-critical driver is exactly what caused the six-week forecast slip. This shows that an average float KPI can hide the single most important signal - which specific path is now driving the finish date - behind an aggregate number that looks reassuring.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly recommends tracking the float of the single most critical (lowest/most negative) path, plus its trend over time, rather than (or in addition to) a schedule-wide average, and recommends a distribution view (e.g., a float histogram or a top-10-lowest-float-paths report) instead of a single blended number for management reporting.
expertAnswer: An expert generalizes this into a broader principle: any aggregate schedule health statistic (average float, percentage critical, BEI, etc.) can mask offsetting movements between paths and should never be the sole KPI relied upon for early warning - they would propose a dashboard combining the critical path's own float trend, the count and identity of paths that have crossed a float threshold since the last period, and the aggregate statistic together, specifically to prevent this kind of masking from recurring.
explanation: A single averaged statistic collapses information across many independent paths into one number, which by construction can hide large offsetting movements. The real driver of the forecast slip - the baggage handling integration path losing most of its float and becoming the new critical or near-critical path - is invisible in the average because a separate path's float gain (from an unrelated early completion) offset it in the aggregate calculation.
reasoning: Average float = sum of all remaining activities' Total Float / count of activities. Because this treats every activity equally and sums across the whole network, a large float loss on one high-count or high-magnitude path can be numerically cancelled out by a large float gain on another path, producing a stable average even though the actual schedule risk profile (which specific path now governs the finish, and how much float it has) has changed dramatically.

subcategory: Retained Logic vs Progress Override
skill: Explaining how identical progress data can produce different forecast finish dates depending on the Retained Logic vs Progress Override scheduling option
scenario: A district cooling plant's mechanical completion activity, 'Pipe Rack Insulation - Zone B', is progressed out of sequence: its successor, 'Pressure Test Zone B', was started and is 40% complete before Pipe Rack Insulation itself finished (Pipe Rack Insulation is 90% complete, with 2 days of Remaining Duration). The scheduler runs the same data-dated update twice - once with the 'Retained Logic' scheduling option and once with 'Progress Override' - and gets two different forecast finish dates for Pressure Test Zone B.
question: Explain, in P6-specific terms, why Retained Logic and Progress Override produce different forecast results for the same out-of-sequence progress data, and which option you would recommend using as standard practice and why.
expectedAnswer: Retained Logic respects the original relationship even when progress has occurred out of sequence: it forces the remaining, unfinished portion of Pressure Test Zone B's work to resume only after Pipe Rack Insulation's Remaining Duration (2 days) is complete, effectively pausing the successor's remaining work until the predecessor logic is satisfied, which pushes Pressure Test Zone B's forecast finish later. Progress Override ignores the predecessor relationship once out-of-sequence progress has started the successor, and calculates the successor's remaining work as continuing uninterrupted from the current data date, without waiting for the predecessor to finish, generally producing an earlier forecast finish. As standard practice, most planning teams and specifications favor Retained Logic (or a hybrid 'Actual Dates' approach with the out-of-sequence condition manually investigated and corrected) because Progress Override can silently mask a real logic problem and produce an overly optimistic forecast.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes that neither option is a substitute for actually investigating why the work went out of sequence in the first place - if Pressure Test can genuinely proceed on the completed portion of pipe rack insulation without needing the remaining 2 days finished, the real fix is often to remodel the relationship (e.g., as SS + lag or split into sub-activities) rather than relying on either scheduling option to paper over an inaccurate logic model.
expertAnswer: An expert flags that many contracts and specifications (and most forensic delay-analysis protocols) require Retained Logic as the default because Progress Override can be used, deliberately or not, to generate a more favorable-looking forecast without addressing the underlying out-of-sequence condition, and that consistent, disclosed use of one option across all updates is essential for update-to-update comparability in any later delay analysis.
explanation: P6's out-of-sequence progress handling options change how the schedule engine treats work that has started before its logical predecessor relationship would normally allow. Retained Logic preserves the relationship's controlling effect on remaining work, generally yielding a later, more conservative forecast; Progress Override effectively suspends the relationship once out-of-sequence progress exists, generally yielding an earlier, less conservative forecast. The two are not equally valid defaults - Retained Logic is the more common, more defensible standard because it does not silently discard logic the schedule was built on.
reasoning: Out-of-sequence progress occurs when a successor activity has actual progress recorded before its predecessor has completed the portion of work the relationship represents. The scheduling engine must decide how to treat the successor's remaining work: Retained Logic keeps the predecessor's remaining duration as a controlling factor on the successor's remaining work (as if the relationship still applies going forward), while Progress Override treats the relationship as satisfied once out-of-sequence progress exists and calculates remaining work independently from the current data date.
commonMistakes: Not knowing the two options exist or how they differ.
Assuming the forecast difference between the two options is a bug rather than a deliberate scheduling engine choice.
Using Progress Override without investigating why out-of-sequence progress occurred in the first place.
redFlags: Candidate cannot explain the mechanical difference between the two options.
Candidate defaults to Progress Override simply because it produces a more favorable date, without justification.
p6Checks: Check the schedule's Out-of-Sequence handling option under Schedule Options (Retained Logic vs Progress Override vs Actual Dates).
Identify all activities currently showing out-of-sequence progress in the update.
Consider remodeling the relationship (SS + lag, or splitting the activity) if the out-of-sequence pattern reflects a genuinely different real-world sequence.

subcategory: Out-of-Sequence Progress Effects
skill: Diagnosing an apparent contradiction where a successor appears ahead of schedule while its predecessor is behind
scenario: In a logistics warehouse fit-out, 'Install Racking System - Bay 4' (predecessor) is 55% complete and two weeks behind its baseline. Its successor, 'Racking Load Test - Bay 4', shows 30% complete and is reported as one week AHEAD of its baseline dates, despite the schedule using Retained Logic for out-of-sequence handling.

expectedAnswer: With Retained Logic, the successor's remaining work is still controlled by the predecessor's remaining duration - so on its face this looks contradictory. The most likely explanation is that this is a case of legitimate out-of-sequence progress rather than a display error: some physical load-testing work in Bay 4 was performed on portions of racking already installed, ahead of the full racking scope finishing, and the small amount of successor progress recorded (30%) reflects real, already-completed work on the tested portion, which the reporting system compared against a baseline date for the whole activity rather than a partial baseline for just the tested portion - creating a misleading 'ahead of schedule' label. Alternatively, the successor's baseline dates themselves may be set generously relative to its own scope, making even modest early progress read as 'ahead' in isolation.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate would specifically pull the out-of-sequence report to confirm whether Racking Load Test shows an out-of-sequence flag, and would check whether its remaining duration or forecast finish (not just percent complete vs baseline start date) is actually favorable once Retained Logic properly re-imposes the predecessor's controlling effect on the remainder of the work.
expertAnswer: An expert cautions against trusting a simple 'ahead/behind baseline' percent-complete comparison in isolation whenever out-of-sequence progress is present, since percent complete does not capture logic constraints - the correct test is whether the successor's forecast (Remaining Duration-driven) finish date, post-Retained-Logic recalculation, is actually favorable, not whether its percent complete looks good against an isolated baseline percentage.
explanation: An apparent contradiction between a delayed predecessor and an 'ahead of schedule' successor, when Retained Logic is genuinely in effect, is most often a reporting artifact of comparing percent-complete-to-baseline in isolation, rather than the forecast finish date after Retained Logic properly reasserts the predecessor's control over the successor's remaining scope. Real progress on the successor is possible even out of sequence (some scope was physically executable ahead of the full predecessor completion), but the schedule engine will still push the successor's forecast finish out once Retained Logic recalculates, so the 'ahead' label typically will not survive a proper look at forecast dates rather than percent complete.
reasoning: Percent complete and 'ahead/behind baseline' status bars are often computed independently of the schedule engine's logic recalculation and can be misleading when out-of-sequence progress exists. The authoritative test of whether the successor is genuinely ahead is its recalculated forecast finish date after applying Retained Logic, which reimposes the predecessor's remaining duration as a control on the successor's remaining work - this is very unlikely to show a genuinely favorable position if the predecessor itself is materially behind.

Not checking for an out-of-sequence flag on the successor activity.
Assuming Retained Logic being 'in use' guarantees the displayed status is already logic-consistent without rerunning the schedule.

Candidate cannot distinguish percent-complete status from forecast-finish status.

subcategory: Float Ownership Between Parallel Paths
skill: Determining whether float consumed on one path affects the float of a genuinely independent parallel path
scenario: A stadium construction schedule has two entirely separate scopes proceeding in parallel toward two different, independent milestones with no shared activities or resources: the seating bowl structure (finishing into 'Seating Bowl Complete') and the pitch drainage and turf installation (finishing into 'Pitch Ready for Handover'). A four-week delay hits the seating bowl structure path and consumes all of its float.
question: Does the seating bowl path consuming all of its float also reduce the float on the pitch drainage/turf path, given that the two paths share no activities? Explain when float would or would not be shared between two paths.
expectedAnswer: No, not automatically. If the two paths are truly independent - no shared activities, no common predecessor or successor tying them together, and each terminates at its own separate milestone with its own separate constraint - then float consumed on one path has no mechanical effect on the other's float. Float would only be shared (i.e., a delay on one path affects the other) if the two paths eventually converge at a common downstream point, such as both being required predecessors to a single overall project finish milestone, or if they compete for the same limited resource (which affects leveled, not logical, float), or if they are linked by any relationship, direct or indirect.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly checks whether both paths are, despite appearing separate, required predecessors of a single overall 'Substantial Completion' or 'Project Finish' milestone - if so, the two paths do share a governing constraint at that convergence point, and depending on how much float each independently has relative to that shared milestone, one path's float loss could still change which path is now more critical relative to that shared finish, even though the two paths' day-to-day activities remain logically unconnected.
expertAnswer: An expert distinguishes 'logical float sharing' (via a common downstream convergence point) from 'resource float sharing' (via competing for the same constrained trade or equipment, revealed only after leveling) and checks both explicitly, since a schedule review that only checks direct logic links could still miss a resource-driven interaction between the two paths.
explanation: Total Float is determined entirely by an activity's own path structure back to whatever constraint governs it. Two paths that share no activities and no common downstream convergence point are mathematically independent in the CPM logic network - a delay and float loss on one has zero effect on the other's calculated Total Float. Float sharing only occurs where paths converge (a common successor or shared finish milestone) or where a resource constraint (only visible after leveling) links them operationally even without a logical tie.
reasoning: Total Float = Late Date - Early Date, computed along a specific chain of relationships. If Path A's chain and Path B's chain never intersect (no shared activity, no common successor), their backward and forward passes are entirely separate calculations with no shared terms, so a change in Path A's float cannot algebraically alter Path B's float. This only breaks down once the two paths converge at a shared downstream point or compete for a shared, leveled resource.
commonMistakes: Assuming any delay anywhere on a project must consume float everywhere.
Not checking for a common downstream convergence point before concluding paths are independent.
Ignoring resource-driven (leveled) interactions between logically unconnected paths.
redFlags: Candidate assumes all float is drawn from one shared 'pool' across the entire project.
Candidate cannot identify what would actually link two paths' float (shared successor or shared resource).
p6Checks: Trace both paths' full predecessor/successor chains to confirm no shared activity or common downstream milestone exists.
Check whether both paths are required predecessors to a single overall project finish activity.
Review resource assignments on both paths for any shared, constrained trade or equipment that leveling might link.

subcategory: Negative Float Hidden From Criticality View
skill: Diagnosing why a project reporting overall negative float can show zero activities visually flagged as critical
scenario: A water treatment plant schedule's status bar reports Project Total Float of -11 days. The Gantt chart, using the project's standard color-coding rule (bars turn red if Total Float <= 0 AND the activity's Status is not 'Completed'), shows no red bars at all - every remaining activity's bar is displayed in the default (non-critical) color.
question: How can a project reporting -11 days of overall Total Float show zero activities visually flagged as critical on the Gantt chart? What would you check first?
expectedAnswer: Most likely, the color-coding bar rule is referencing the wrong float field, is misconfigured, or has not been refreshed after the last schedule recalculation - for example, the bar chart's conditional formatting might be referencing a stale/cached Total Float value, referencing Free Float instead of Total Float by mistake, or the color rule's threshold was typed incorrectly (e.g., 'Total Float < 0' using a data type that does not evaluate negative float correctly, or comparing against the wrong baseline). It is also possible the schedule was not actually recalculated (F9) after the -11 days was reported, so the Gantt is displaying dates/float from a prior calculation cycle.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate lays out a specific, ordered checklist: first confirm the schedule has been recalculated since the last data entry, then inspect the bar/color coding rule's exact field reference and operator, then manually sort the Activities table by Total Float ascending to see the true numeric picture independent of the Gantt's visual formatting.
expertAnswer: An expert treats this as a reporting-integrity issue requiring root-cause correction before any further client reporting proceeds, since a visual tool this fundamentally broken could have been silently misrepresenting criticality in every report issued since the formatting rule was last correct - they would recommend a full audit of when this discrepancy began and whether any prior period's report relied on the broken visual.
explanation: A Gantt chart's color coding is a display rule applied on top of the underlying calculated data; it can become disconnected from the true Total Float values through a misconfigured field reference, an incorrect threshold operator, a rule referencing a different float type, or simply displaying stale data because the schedule was not recalculated after the last change. The -11 days reported in the status bar is the authoritative CPM output; the absence of red bars is a display/configuration defect, not evidence the float figure is wrong.
reasoning: Total Float is calculated during the schedule's forward/backward pass and stored per activity; the status bar summary reads directly from this. A bar color rule, by contrast, is a separately configured conditional format that must correctly reference the Total Float field, use a correct comparison operator, and operate on current (recalculated) data to display accurately - any one of those being wrong produces exactly this kind of silent visual failure without affecting the underlying numeric float values at all.
commonMistakes: Assuming the Total Float figure in the status bar must be wrong because the Gantt shows no red bars.
Not checking whether the schedule was recalculated after the underlying data changed.
Not inspecting the exact field and operator used in the color-coding rule.
redFlags: Candidate cannot propose a systematic diagnostic sequence.
Candidate assumes this is simply cosmetic and not worth investigating further.

Open the Bar/Gantt chart's conditional formatting or bar style rules and verify the field reference (Total Float, not Free Float) and operator.

subcategory: Decomposition Revealing Hidden Concurrency
skill: Explaining how breaking a single long-duration activity into detailed sub-activities can legitimately shorten the calculated critical path with no scope change
scenario: An offshore platform topside module fabrication schedule originally modeled 'Fabricate and Paint Module Skid' as one 60-day activity, Finish-to-Start into 'Load Out'. In a schedule revision, the planner breaks this into 'Fabricate Structural Frame' (35 days), 'Mechanical/Piping Fit-up' (25 days, Start-to-Start + 10-day lag from Fabricate Structural Frame), and 'Paint and Coating' (12 days, Start-to-Start + 5-day lag from Mechanical/Piping Fit-up), with Load Out now following Paint and Coating's finish. The critical path through this section shortens from 60 days to 47 days, with no scope, resource, or duration-per-unit change.
question: Is a 13-day reduction in critical path length legitimate here, given that no scope or resource change occurred? Explain the mechanism.
expectedAnswer: Yes, this can be entirely legitimate. The original single 60-day activity implicitly modeled the three trades as fully sequential (nothing could start until the whole prior activity finished), which understated the real achievable concurrency between structural fabrication, mechanical fit-up, and painting - trades that, in reality, can and do overlap once enough of the preceding work is complete. Decomposing the activity into its real components and modeling the true overlap (via Start-to-Start relationships with realistic lags) reveals concurrency that was always physically achievable but was hidden by the coarse, single-bar modeling of the original activity - this is a schedule quality improvement, not an artificial compression.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate is careful to distinguish this from an unsubstantiated 'recovery schedule' compression (as in a scenario where durations are cut with no basis) - here, the total scope of work and durations for each real trade remain unchanged (35 + lag structure is consistent with real achievable overlap), and the reduction comes purely from more accurately representing already-true physical concurrency, which is verifiable against the individual trade durations and lags shown.
expertAnswer: An expert would still want to verify the specific lags (10-day and 5-day) against a real constructability basis (e.g., how much structural frame must be complete before mechanical fit-up can safely start) rather than accepting the improvement at face value just because it is more granular - decomposition can also be misused to introduce unrealistic overlap dressed up as 'detail', so the underlying lag justification still needs scrutiny even though the general technique is legitimate.
explanation: A single coarse activity forces full sequential logic on everything nested inside it, even where real trades can overlap. Decomposing that activity into its real constituent scopes and modeling the true, physically achievable overlap between them with appropriate lag values is a standard, legitimate way to improve schedule accuracy and can genuinely shorten the calculated critical path without changing total scope, total labor hours, or per-trade durations - because the original single-activity model was simply less accurate, not because any real acceleration occurred.
reasoning: Under the original model, Load Out could not start until all 60 days of combined work were shown as finished sequentially. Under the decomposed model, mechanical fit-up genuinely starts 10 days after structural fabrication begins (not after it fully finishes), and painting genuinely starts 5 days after fit-up begins, reflecting real trade sequencing practice; the critical path length becomes 35 + 10 + 25(remaining portion accounted through lag) ... effectively the longest path through the decomposed chain, which is shorter than the artificially sequential 60-day sum specifically because true overlap is now represented.
commonMistakes: Assuming any reduction in critical path length without added resources must be illegitimate compression.
Not distinguishing decomposition-revealed concurrency from an unsubstantiated duration cut.
Accepting the new lags without checking their constructability basis.
redFlags: Candidate treats this exactly the same as an unjustified recovery schedule without recognizing the different underlying mechanism.
Candidate cannot explain why the original single-activity model overstated true duration.
p6Checks: Compare the decomposed activities' individual durations against the trades' known productivity rates for consistency.
Verify the SS lag values against a documented constructability basis for how much predecessor work must complete before the successor can start.
Confirm total resource-hours are unchanged between the old single activity and the new decomposed set.

subcategory: EOT Granted Yet Float Decreases
skill: Explaining how a granted Extension of Time can be followed by a decrease, not increase, in overall project Total Float
scenario: On a government roadway widening contract, the contractor is granted a 20-day Extension of Time for an owner-caused utility conflict, and the contract completion milestone's constraint date is formally revised 20 days later. Immediately after this revision is incorporated into the schedule, the project's overall Total Float, which had been -8 days before the EOT, becomes -15 days after the EOT is incorporated - a worse position, not an improved one.
question: How can incorporating a granted 20-day EOT make the project's overall Total Float worse rather than better? Is this technically possible, and what would you check first?
expectedAnswer: Yes, this is possible. Total Float only improves as much as the EOT actually extends the specific constraint governing the currently controlling (most critical) path. If, in the same period the EOT was being processed, the contractor incurred additional culpable (contractor-caused) delay or other, separately unextended delay on the controlling path - for example, a subcontractor mobilization delay, a design coordination issue, or slower-than-planned progress on other critical scope - that new delay could consume more float than the 20-day EOT restored, producing a net worse position. It is also possible the EOT was granted and applied to a different (non-controlling) milestone or a specific interim section, not the overall contract completion constraint that is actually driving the reported project Total Float.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly separates the mechanical CPM check (did the 20 days actually get applied to the constraint governing the currently critical path, and was any other, unrelated delay incorporated in the same update) from the commercial/contractual question (is the newly-revealed worse position now a basis for a further EOT claim, subject to notice and causation requirements under the specific contract).
expertAnswer: An expert flags this as a classic scenario requiring a clean, well-documented time-impact analysis separating the EOT-related schedule change from any concurrent, unrelated schedule changes incorporated in the same update - failing to separate them risks either overstating the contractor's remaining entitlement (if unrelated culpable delay is conflated with the EOT event) or understating the owner's exposure (if a further legitimate delay is masked by the EOT's apparent improvement) - and would insist any further claim be supported by its own discrete causation and quantification, never inferred simply from the net float change.
explanation: An EOT changes one specific input - typically the constraint date on the contract completion milestone (or the relevant interim milestone) - by the granted number of days. It does not freeze or protect every other input to the schedule in the same period; if additional delay (contractor-caused, concurrent, or otherwise) was incorporated in the same update on the path that actually governs the reported project Total Float, that additional consumption can exceed the 20-day benefit of the EOT, producing a net worse Total Float position. The EOT and the additional delay are two separate, independently occurring changes; nothing guarantees they net to an improvement.
reasoning: Before the EOT: Total Float = -8 days, reflecting the constraint date minus the (unextended) forecast finish along the controlling path. After the EOT: the constraint date moves 20 days later, which alone would improve Total Float to +12 days, but if in the same update the forecast finish along the controlling path also moved later by, say, 27 days (due to newly incorporated, unrelated or concurrent delay), the net result is -15 days (+12 - 27 = -15). Both changes are real and independently verifiable; the EOT did exactly what it was meant to do, but a larger, separate delay outpaced it in the same period.
commonMistakes: Assuming a granted EOT must always improve or at minimum not worsen the project's Total Float position.
Conflating the EOT-related schedule change with other, unrelated changes incorporated in the same update.
Assuming the -15 days automatically entitles the contractor to a further EOT without separate causation analysis.
redFlags: Candidate assumes the worse float position means the EOT was calculated incorrectly.
Candidate does not separate the EOT's mechanical effect from other delay incorporated in the same update.
Candidate jumps to entitlement conclusions without referencing contract-specific notice and causation requirements.
p6Checks: Isolate the schedule fragnet/change specifically attributable to the EOT-granted constraint revision from all other changes made in the same update.
Identify what else changed on the controlling path in this update period (new delays, logic revisions, progress updates).
Recalculate Total Float with only the EOT change applied, in isolation, to confirm the 20-day benefit was correctly implemented.

subcategory: Diminishing Returns from Added Resources
skill: Explaining why doubling crew size on a critical activity can fail to shorten the project finish date
scenario: In a confined tunnel section (single-face heading), the project manager doubles the excavation crew size on the critical activity 'Excavate and Support - Chainage 400-600' hoping to halve its 30-day duration. After the change, the activity's actual duration barely improves, finishing in 27 days, and the project finish date does not move at all.
question: Why would doubling the crew size on a critical, single-face tunnel excavation activity fail to meaningfully shorten its duration or the project finish?
expectedAnswer: In a confined, single-face working environment, only a limited number of workers can physically and safely occupy the heading at once - beyond that physical limit, additional labor cannot increase output and can even reduce it through congestion, interference, and safety constraints (the tunnel face has a fixed working area). Excavation and support progress is governed by cycle time (drill, blast/excavate, muck out, support installation) rather than by total headcount, so doubling the crew does not double the rate of advance when the constraint is physical space and cycle sequencing, not labor availability. Additionally, if the project finish date did not move even after some improvement (30 to 27 days), the activity may not have actually been on the sole critical path, or another path/constraint (e.g., muck disposal logistics, ventilation cycle time, or a downstream activity's own float) absorbed the 3-day gain without it reaching the finish date.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly separates two distinct reasons: (1) the physical/space constraint limiting how much added labor can genuinely accelerate a confined single-face operation, and (2) the possibility that even the modest 3-day gain achieved did not translate to the project finish because of float absorption elsewhere or a resource-critical (not logic-critical) constraint like muck removal capacity.
expertAnswer: An expert connects this to the general project management principle that adding resources to a task has diminishing, and eventually negative, returns once a task's true constraint is not labor availability but a fixed process/cycle-time or physical-space limit (directly analogous to the well-known principle that adding manpower to a late task does not linearly accelerate it, and can even slow it through congestion) - and would recommend attacking the actual constraint (parallel headings, longer shifts, faster muck-out logistics, or improved cycle sequencing) rather than crew size as the lever for genuine acceleration.
explanation: A single-face tunnel excavation is a cycle-time-constrained, space-constrained operation: excavation, mucking, and support each require sequential steps in a fixed physical area, and only so many workers can be productively engaged in each step at once. Adding workers beyond that physical/process limit does not shorten the cycle time and can introduce congestion that partially offsets any small gain, which is consistent with the modest 27-day result. Separately, even the modest improvement achieved may not have reached the project finish date if the activity was not the sole driver of the critical path, or if a different (resource- or logistics-driven) constraint downstream absorbed the gain.
reasoning: Duration for a cycle-constrained activity is a function of the number of repeatable cycles required and the fixed cycle time per unit of advance, not simply total labor-hours divided by crew size, once the physical work area is saturated. Because tunnel heading space is finite, doubling the crew adds workers who cannot be usefully engaged in the same cycle step simultaneously, so the theoretical halving of duration (labor-hours-based logic) does not materialize; the schedule impact caps out near the physical/process limit regardless of added headcount.
commonMistakes: Assuming duration is always inversely proportional to crew size (linear productivity assumption).
Not recognizing physical space or cycle-time constraints as independent limits on achievable acceleration.
Not checking whether the activity was genuinely the sole driver of the project finish date.
redFlags: Candidate assumes any added resource must proportionally shorten duration.
Candidate cannot identify physical/space or cycle-time constraints as a limiting factor distinct from labor availability.
p6Checks: Review the activity's resource-loading assumptions and productivity basis (units/day per crew) used at baseline versus what is physically achievable in the confined heading.
Confirm whether this activity was genuinely the sole critical driver of the project finish, or one of several paths.
Check downstream logistics (muck disposal, ventilation cycle) for an independent constraint that may be the true limiting factor.

subcategory: Float Consumed Faster Than the Delay Event
skill: Explaining how a delay smaller than an activity's available float can still immediately shift the project finish date
scenario: An offshore wind farm cable-laying schedule shows the activity 'Inter-Array Cable Pull - String 6' with 38 days of Total Float. String 6 slips by only 10 days due to a vessel scheduling issue. Despite having 28 days of float remaining even after the slip, the project's forecast finish date moves out by 10 days immediately in the same update.
question: Is it possible for a delay smaller than an activity's available float to still immediately shift the project finish date? If so, explain how, given that logically this activity still shows 28 days of float remaining.
expectedAnswer: Yes, this is possible when the activity's Total Float, as calculated by the logical CPM network, does not reflect an independent real-world constraint that also governs the same window - most plausibly here, a fixed marine work window (e.g., cable-laying vessel availability is contractually or seasonally limited to a specific weather window that is about to close). If the 10-day slip pushes String 6's cable pull past the point where the specialized vessel is available (due to a fixed mobilization/demobilization schedule or seasonal weather restriction), the project finish is driven by that external, calendar-bound constraint, not by the logical float shown in the CPM network, so a 10-day slip can force a full re-mobilization delay (e.g., waiting for the vessel's next available window) that is much larger than the raw 10-day slip and unrelated to the 28 days of 'float' still shown.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate specifically identifies that the calculated Total Float assumes continuous resource/vessel availability, which may not hold if a marine spread or specialist vessel is only booked/available for a fixed window - the CPM float number is 'logically' accurate but does not capture this external, resource-availability constraint unless it is explicitly modeled as a constraint or calendar restriction on the activity.
expertAnswer: An expert would treat this as evidence the schedule is under-modeled for the real operational constraint (vessel availability windows should be represented as calendars or constraints directly on the relevant activities, not left implicit), and would recommend adding an explicit vessel availability calendar or constraint to the schedule so that future updates correctly reflect this risk in the calculated float, rather than relying on planners to remember an unmodeled real-world limitation each time.
explanation: Total Float, as calculated purely from logical relationships and durations, assumes the resources needed to execute an activity remain available for as long as its calculated late dates allow. When a real, external constraint - such as a fixed marine work window governed by vessel contract terms or seasonal weather restrictions - is not explicitly represented in the schedule (via a calendar or constraint), the calculated float can overstate the activity's true schedule flexibility. If the 10-day slip pushes the activity past the actual availability window, the real-world impact (losing the vessel and waiting for the next window) can be far larger than what the CPM float number implies, and can hit the project finish date immediately once that external constraint is breached.
reasoning: The 28 days of remaining calculated float describes slack relative to the logical network's late dates, not relative to any unmodeled external resource constraint. If the specialized cable-laying vessel's actual availability window closes in, say, 8 days from the original planned start, then a 10-day slip breaches that window regardless of the 38 days of logical float, and the consequence (waiting for the next available window, potentially months away in a seasonal marine environment) is what actually drives the forecast finish date, not the CPM-calculated float.
commonMistakes: Assuming calculated Total Float always fully captures real-world schedule flexibility.
Not checking for unmodeled external constraints (vessel windows, seasonal restrictions, permit windows) separate from logical float.
Concluding the schedule software must have made an error when the forecast finish moves despite apparent float.
redFlags: Candidate cannot conceive of a real-world constraint operating outside the logical CPM network.
Candidate insists the forecast finish move must be a software error given the float shown.
p6Checks: Check whether the specialized vessel's availability window is represented as a calendar restriction or constraint on String 6 and related activities.
Review the marine spread/vessel contract or mobilization schedule for the actual availability window versus the activity's calculated late dates.
Consider adding an explicit constraint or specialized calendar to correctly reflect this limitation in future updates.

subcategory: Removing Redundant-Looking Logic Shortens the Path
skill: Explaining how removing a seemingly redundant logic tie can legitimately shorten the critical path
scenario: In a residential tower schedule, a relationship links 'MEP Rough-In - Level 12' to 'Drywall Installation - Level 12' with a Finish-to-Start relationship, in addition to the already-existing chain through 'MEP Inspection - Level 12' (which itself precedes Drywall). A schedule review determines the direct MEP Rough-In to Drywall link is logically redundant, since the inspection activity already sits between them, and removes it. The critical path shortens by 15 days.
question: If the removed relationship was 'redundant' (the same constraint was already enforced through the inspection activity), how can removing it shorten the critical path by 15 days?
expectedAnswer: The relationship was not actually fully redundant in float terms, even though it looked logically unnecessary at first glance - it likely carried a longer effective lag or a different relationship type (or represented a stricter, more conservative constraint) than the path through the inspection activity, meaning it was, in practice, the more restrictive (governing) of the two ties. Removing it left only the less restrictive path (through inspection) governing the successor's start, which had genuinely more available time - hence the 15-day reduction. What looked redundant in terms of logical existence (both paths eventually reach Drywall) was not redundant in terms of numerical restrictiveness.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate is careful to check this was a legitimate finding (the direct link truly was over-restrictive relative to the inspection path) rather than an error - they would verify the inspection activity path genuinely still enforces the necessary real-world sequencing (drywall cannot start before MEP is inspected and approved) before accepting the 15-day improvement as valid.
expertAnswer: An expert cautions that 'redundant-looking' relationships should be investigated, not deleted, purely because they appear duplicative - the correct process is to verify which of the two ties is more restrictive and confirm the less restrictive one still enforces all necessary real-world constraints, since indiscriminately deleting relationships that look redundant is a known way schedules get inappropriately compressed while looking like a legitimate 'schedule quality cleanup'.
explanation: Two relationships reaching the same successor from a common ancestor are only truly redundant if they impose identical restrictiveness (same effective governing date). Here, the direct MEP Rough-In to Drywall Finish-to-Start relationship was, in practice, more restrictive than the indirect path through inspection - perhaps because inspection could start immediately after rough-in with minimal lag while the direct tie effectively demanded a longer buffer, or the direct tie used a stricter relationship type. Removing the more restrictive of two paths to the same successor, when the less restrictive one still legitimately enforces the necessary sequence, is a valid logic cleanup that can shorten the calculated critical path.
reasoning: A successor's Early Start is governed by the LATEST of all its predecessors' calculated early finish (plus lag) values, i.e., the most restrictive predecessor path controls. If Path 1 (direct MEP-to-Drywall) yields a later required start date for Drywall than Path 2 (via inspection), Path 1 was silently the true governing constraint despite looking redundant on a logic diagram; deleting it removes the more restrictive requirement, and Drywall's early start (and everything downstream) can now be governed by the genuinely less restrictive inspection path, shortening the calculated critical path.
commonMistakes: Assuming any two relationships reaching the same successor must be equally restrictive if both exist.
Deleting a 'redundant-looking' relationship without checking which one actually governs the calculated date.
Not verifying the remaining relationship still enforces the necessary real-world constraint after deletion.
redFlags: Candidate cannot explain why one of two paths to the same successor can be more restrictive than the other.
Candidate treats logic cleanup exercises as risk-free without verification.

Confirm the surviving relationship (via inspection) still enforces the real-world requirement that drywall cannot start before MEP inspection approval.

subcategory: Calendar Effects on Finish Dates
skill: Explaining how a schedule with a longer critical path duration can still finish on an earlier calendar date than a shorter one
scenario: Two competing subcontractor programs are submitted for the same scope of work. Program A's critical path totals 140 working days. Program B's critical path totals 128 working days. Program A is built on a 6-day-per-week calendar; Program B is built on a standard 5-day-per-week calendar, with both starting on the same date.
question: Given these calendars, which program is more likely to reach its calculated finish on an earlier real calendar date?

options.label: A
options.text: Program B, because 128 working days is fewer than 140 working days, and working-day duration always determines the earlier calendar finish regardless of calendar.

options.label: B
options.text: Program A, because 140 working days on a 6-day week consumes roughly 163 calendar days, while 128 working days on a 5-day week consumes roughly 179 calendar days, so Program A actually finishes earlier in real calendar time despite the longer working-day total.

options.label: C
options.text: They are guaranteed to finish on the same calendar date because both start on the same date and calendar differences do not affect the finish date, only the intermediate float values.

options.label: D
options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the total cost of each program.

explanation: Working-day duration is not directly comparable across schedules built on different calendars, because the number of real calendar days consumed by a given number of working days depends entirely on how many working days occur per calendar week. Program A's 140 working days on a 6-day calendar consume roughly 140 / 6 x 7 ≈ 163 calendar days, while Program B's 128 working days on a 5-day calendar consume roughly 128 / 5 x 7 ≈ 179 calendar days - so despite having a 'longer' schedule by working-day count, Program A finishes earlier in real time because it works more days per week.
reasoning: A schedule's working-day critical path length must always be converted to calendar days using its specific calendar's working pattern before two schedules on different calendars can be meaningfully compared for real finish dates. Comparing raw working-day totals across differing calendars, without this conversion, is a common and consequential planning error - one of the most basic due-diligence checks when comparing competing programs or claims that reference 'days' without specifying calendar basis.
commonMistakes: Comparing working-day totals directly across schedules without checking each one's calendar.
Assuming 'fewer working days' always means 'finishes sooner' in real time.
Not asking what calendar (5-day, 6-day, 7-day) a stated duration is based on before comparing it to another schedule.
redFlags: Candidate compares working-day totals across programs without asking about their respective calendars.
Candidate cannot perform the working-day-to-calendar-day conversion.
p6Checks: Check the calendar assigned to each program's critical path activities (5-day, 6-day, or 7-day working week, and holiday exceptions).
Convert each program's working-day critical path length to calendar days for a true apples-to-apples comparison.
Verify actual calculated finish dates directly from each schedule rather than relying on working-day totals alone.

subcategory: Positive Total Float Yet LD Exposure
skill: Reconciling positive overall project Total Float with looming liquidated damages exposure on a sectional milestone
scenario: On an EPC substation package, the overall project Total Float (relative to the final contract completion date) is +15 days. However, the contract contains a Sectional Completion milestone for 'Energization of Bay 3' with its own liquidated damages provision, and that milestone's Total Float, calculated relative to its own contractual date, is -9 days.
question: How can the project show +15 days of overall Total Float while the contractor is already facing liquidated damages exposure? Is this a contradiction?
expectedAnswer: This is not a contradiction. Total Float is calculated relative to whatever constraint governs the specific path being measured; the overall project Total Float of +15 days is measured against the final contract completion date, while the Bay 3 energization sectional milestone has its own separate contractual date and its own separate LD provision, against which its path is already running -9 days. A project can have healthy float on its way to overall final completion while simultaneously being behind, and financially exposed, on an interim contractual milestone with its own independent deadline and consequences.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly notes that whether the overall project float is 'shared', 'contractor-owned', or otherwise governed is itself a matter of the specific contract's float-ownership clause, and that this does not change the separate, independent fact of the Bay 3 sectional LD exposure - these are two different contractual mechanisms that must each be tracked and reported separately, not netted against each other.
expertAnswer: An expert emphasizes that reporting only the headline +15 days overall float, without separately flagging the Bay 3 sectional exposure, would be a materially misleading representation of the project's actual commercial risk position, and recommends that any project controls report explicitly track and disclose every contractual milestone with its own LD or sectional completion provision as a distinct line, independent of overall project float, since a client or board relying only on the aggregate figure could be blindsided by a sectional LD claim.
explanation: Overall project Total Float and a specific sectional milestone's Total Float are two independently calculated numbers, each relative to its own governing constraint (final completion date vs the Bay 3 contractual energization date). Contracts with sectional completion clauses create genuinely separate deadlines, each carrying its own consequences (LDs specific to that section) regardless of how comfortable the overall project position looks. There is no requirement, contractual or mathematical, that these two figures move together or offset each other.
reasoning: The overall +15 days reflects that the path driving final contract completion currently has slack. The Bay 3 path's -9 days reflects that the specific chain of activities required to energize Bay 3 by its own contractual date is already behind. These are different paths (different sets of activities) measured against different constraint dates; nothing in CPM logic forces a project's overall float to bound or predict every sectional milestone's float individually.
commonMistakes: Assuming positive overall project float means no part of the project can be behind schedule.
Reporting only the aggregate float figure without separately tracking sectional milestone exposure.
Assuming LD exposure on a sectional milestone can be offset by overall project float.
redFlags: Candidate treats the +15 days as proof there is no commercial risk anywhere on the project.
Candidate cannot explain that sectional completion milestones carry independent contractual consequences.
p6Checks: Identify all sectional/interim completion milestones in the contract and confirm each has its own constraint date correctly modeled in the schedule.
Calculate Total Float independently for each sectional milestone's own governing path, not just the overall project finish.
Cross-reference each sectional milestone's LD provision against its currently calculated float trend.

subcategory: Cost-Based Schedule Variance vs Time-Based Delay
skill: Reconciling a positive dollar-based Schedule Variance with a CPM analysis showing the project behind on the critical path
scenario: On a chemical plant EPC project, at the current data date, PV = $18,500,000 and EV = $19,200,000, giving a Schedule Variance (SV) of +$700,000 - favorable, in dollar terms. A parallel CPM-based schedule analysis of the same period shows the critical path has slipped by 11 days versus the baseline.
question: Calculate SV in dollars, then explain how the project can show a favorable dollar-based Schedule Variance while independently confirmed critical-path analysis shows an 11-day slip.
explanation: SV = EV - PV = 19,200,000 - 18,500,000 = +$700,000 (favorable). Dollar-based SV, like SPI, is a blended, budget-weighted measure of work volume completed against work planned - it reflects the earned value of ALL work performed to date, not specifically the value of critical-path work. A project can earn more dollar-value than planned overall (e.g., by getting ahead on high-budget, float-rich procurement or bulk-commodity installation) while simultaneously falling behind on lower-budget but zero-float critical-path activities (e.g., a specific vessel delivery or a permit-gated tie-in), producing a favorable blended SV alongside a genuine critical-path slip.
reasoning: SV in dollars aggregates variance across the entire cost-loaded scope regardless of which activities are critical. If, for example, $2.1M of favorable variance came from float-rich bulk piping and equipment installation running ahead of plan, while $1.4M of unfavorable variance came from a small but critical-path-driving vessel delivery and tie-in package running behind, the net blended SV is still +$700,000 favorable, even though the specific activities driving the finish date are the ones running behind. Only a CPM trace of the critical path (or an EVM calculation restricted specifically to critical-path activities) reveals the true date impact; the blended dollar SV cannot.
commonMistakes: Reporting a favorable SV as proof the project is on or ahead of schedule without checking the CPM critical path.
Not recognizing that SV is budget-weighted and blind to which specific activities are critical.
Assuming SV and CPM-based schedule slippage must always agree in sign.
redFlags: Uses a favorable SV to dismiss or downplay a confirmed CPM critical-path slip.
Cannot explain that SV aggregates across all cost-loaded scope regardless of criticality.

subcategory: High Task-Hit-Rate Masking Critical Delay
skill: Recognizing that a high percentage of on-time tasks can coexist with a late overall forecast when the missed tasks are the high-impact ones
scenario: A rail signaling installation project reports that 94% of scheduled tasks were completed on or ahead of their baseline dates this period. Despite this strong hit rate, the project's overall forecast completion has slipped by five weeks versus baseline.
question: How can a 94% on-time task completion rate coexist with a five-week slip in the overall forecast finish? What does this suggest about how task-hit-rate metrics should be used?
expectedAnswer: The 6% of tasks that were missed are most likely the ones that actually drive the critical path or a high-impact interim milestone (for example, a specific signaling system integration test, a specialist commissioning engineer's availability, or a regulatory approval gate), while the 94% that were completed on time are largely non-critical, float-rich tasks whose timeliness has no bearing on the overall finish date. A raw hit-rate percentage counts tasks equally regardless of their schedule impact, so it can look excellent while the handful of tasks that actually matter for the finish date are exactly the ones that slipped.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate recommends weighting or filtering the hit-rate metric by criticality (e.g., reporting hit rate separately for critical-path tasks versus all tasks) so that the metric cannot be inflated by a large volume of low-impact, on-time work masking a small number of high-impact misses.
expertAnswer: An expert connects this to a broader principle in schedule health metrics: any metric that counts tasks (or activities) without weighting by schedule impact - such as raw hit rate, or a simple percentage of activities completed - is vulnerable to exactly this kind of masking, and recommends always pairing a volume-based metric (like hit rate) with an impact-based one (like critical path slip or float trend) before drawing a conclusion about schedule health from either alone.
explanation: Task hit-rate metrics treat every task as equally weighted, one task, one vote, regardless of whether it sits on the critical path or carries 60 days of float. A project can perform very well on the large majority of non-critical scope while missing the few critical-path-driving tasks, producing a headline metric (94% on time) that looks excellent while the metric that actually matters for delivery (the forecast finish date) tells a much worse story.
reasoning: If 200 tasks were scheduled this period and 188 completed on time (94%), but the 12 that missed included the signaling system integration test and a critical commissioning gate, the forecast finish is driven entirely by those 12 tasks' impact on the critical path, not by the volume of unrelated tasks that happened to finish on time. Hit rate is a volume statistic; forecast finish is an impact statistic; they measure fundamentally different things and are not expected to move together.
commonMistakes: Treating a high task hit-rate percentage as proof of good overall schedule performance.
Not distinguishing critical-path task performance from overall task performance in reporting.
Assuming the two metrics (hit rate and forecast finish) must be consistent with each other.
redFlags: Candidate reports the 94% figure as reassuring without investigating which specific tasks were missed.
Candidate cannot explain why a volume-based metric can diverge from an impact-based one.
p6Checks: Identify which of the 6% missed tasks are on or near the critical path.
Recalculate hit rate restricted to critical-path (or near-critical) tasks only, for comparison.
Trace the five-week forecast slip to its specific driving tasks and cross-reference against the missed-task list.

subcategory: More Accurate Logic Reducing Critical Path Length
skill: Explaining how correcting relationship types to more accurately reflect real sequencing can reduce, not increase, the calculated critical path
scenario: In an MEP coordination schedule for a commercial fit-out, a logic review finds that 'Duct Installation - Zone 2' was linked to 'Duct Insulation - Zone 2' via Finish-to-Start, when in practice insulation crews can and routinely do follow behind duct installation crews at a fixed offset without waiting for the entire zone's ductwork to finish. The planner corrects the relationship to Start-to-Start with an 8-day lag. The critical path shortens by 12 days.
question: The schedule now has what looks like a 'tighter', more constrained relationship (SS + lag instead of a simple FS). Why did adding this more specific logic reduce the critical path length rather than increase it?
expectedAnswer: The original Finish-to-Start relationship was actually the more restrictive (and less accurate) of the two, because it forced Duct Insulation to wait for the entire Duct Installation activity to finish before starting anything, even though real practice allows insulation to begin following behind installation crews well before the whole zone is done. Replacing FS with SS + 8-day lag more accurately represents genuine achievable overlap, which is inherently less restrictive than the artificial full-sequential FS relationship it replaced - hence the critical path shortens. The correction is not 'looser logic', it is 'more accurate logic that happens to allow more real overlap than the oversimplified original model permitted'.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes this is a common schedule-quality improvement pattern: FS relationships are the simplest to build but often overstate true sequential dependency for trades that can legitimately follow one another at an offset, and correcting these to SS/FF with appropriate lag is a standard, defensible schedule accuracy improvement, provided the lag value is itself justified.
expertAnswer: An expert would want to see the 8-day lag justified against real crew productivity and safe working-distance/curing requirements between the two trades, and would flag that while this specific correction is legitimate, the same technique (loosening FS relationships to SS + lag) can also be misused to artificially compress a schedule if the lag is set too aggressively without a genuine constructability basis - so each such change should be reviewed individually on its merits, not accepted as a category.
explanation: A Finish-to-Start relationship, by definition, is the most restrictive way to sequence two activities - the successor cannot start at all until the predecessor's entire scope is finished. If the real-world relationship between two trades is actually an overlapping one (the successor can follow behind the predecessor at a defined offset), modeling it as FS overstates the true dependency and artificially lengthens the calculated critical path. Correcting the relationship to SS with an appropriate lag brings the model in line with reality and, because the real relationship is inherently less restrictive than full FS sequencing, legitimately shortens the calculated critical path.
reasoning: Under FS logic, Duct Insulation's early start = Duct Installation's early finish (the full zone). Under SS + 8-day lag, Duct Insulation's early start = Duct Installation's early start + 8 days, which is earlier than waiting for the full zone's finish (assuming Duct Installation's own duration exceeds 8 days), directly shortening the calculated span for this section of the network and any critical path running through it.
commonMistakes: Assuming any change to relationship type/lag that shortens the critical path must be an artificial compression.
Not recognizing that FS relationships can overstate true sequential dependency for overlapping trades.
Accepting the new lag value without checking its constructability basis.
redFlags: Candidate cannot explain why FS is inherently more restrictive than SS + lag for genuinely overlapping work.
Candidate treats this exactly like an unjustified duration cut without recognizing the different, legitimate mechanism.

Confirm the change is documented in the schedule basis/logic revision log with its constructability justification.
Check for other FS relationships in the schedule between trades that could plausibly overlap, as a broader schedule quality review.

subcategory: Physical vs Duration-Based Progress Governing EVM
skill: Deciding which of two conflicting percent-complete figures should govern earned value on a dredging progress claim
scenario: On a marine capital dredging project, the activity 'Dredge and Disposal - Reach 3' shows Duration % Complete of 82% in P6 (based on elapsed working days against planned duration). The site surveyor's independently measured bathymetric survey, comparing dredged volume against design volume, shows only 61% of the required material has actually been removed.
question: Which figure - 82% duration complete or 61% surveyed volume complete - should govern the monthly progress payment claim and earned value calculation, and why?
expectedAnswer: The 61% surveyed volume figure should govern. Progress payments and earned value should be based on actual, independently verifiable physical output (in this case, measured dredged volume against design volume) rather than elapsed duration, which only reflects time consumed against a planned rate that has evidently not been achieved. Using the 82% duration-based figure would overstate progress and could result in overpayment relative to work actually performed.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes the gap between the two figures (82% vs 61%) is itself important diagnostic information about productivity - dredging rate is running well below the planned rate - and recommends re-forecasting Remaining Duration for Reach 3 using the demonstrated actual production rate rather than leaving it based on the original planned rate.
expertAnswer: An expert additionally flags the contractual dimension: most dredging and earthworks contracts specifically require surveyed/measured quantities (not elapsed time) as the basis for progress payment precisely because duration-based percent complete is well known to overstate output when productivity underperforms, and would check the specific measurement and payment clause in the contract to confirm survey-based measurement governs, while also using the 61% figure (not 82%) in any EVM calculation feeding SPI/CPI to keep those indices meaningful.
explanation: Duration % Complete is a proxy based on elapsed time against planned duration; it implicitly assumes the planned production rate is being achieved and will overstate true progress whenever actual productivity falls short. Physical/surveyed percent complete, based on directly measured output (dredged volume against design volume via independent bathymetric survey), is a much more reliable and typically contractually required basis for both progress payment and earned value, because it reflects what was actually accomplished rather than how much time has passed.
reasoning: If Reach 3's planned production rate assumed a certain volume per working day, and 82% of planned duration has elapsed but only 61% of the design volume has actually been removed, then actual productivity to date is running at roughly 61/82 ≈ 74% of the planned rate. Using 82% for payment or earned value would pay for, or 'earn', roughly 21 percentage points of work that has not actually been performed - a material and, in most contracts, contractually incorrect basis for measurement.
commonMistakes: Using duration percent complete as the default basis for progress payment without checking the contract's measurement clause.
Not reconciling P6's calculated percent complete against independently surveyed/measured quantities.
Leaving Remaining Duration unadjusted despite clear evidence of an underperforming production rate.
redFlags: Candidate recommends paying or reporting against the higher (duration-based) figure without questioning it.
Candidate does not check the contract's measurement and payment basis before deciding.

subcategory: Contemporaneous Updating and Data Integrity
skill: Recognizing that an unrecorded suspension period reveals a data integrity problem rather than an absence of schedule impact
scenario: A retail mall fit-out subcontractor's scope was suspended for three weeks due to unusually severe weather warnings issued by the local authority. The schedule was not updated at all during the suspension - the next update was issued five weeks later, showing progress as if work had continued uninterrupted, with no calendar exception, no suspension activity, and no narrative reference to the stoppage anywhere in the update.
question: Does the fact that the current schedule shows no Total Float consumption or critical path impact from this suspension mean the suspension had no schedule effect? What would you check, and what does the absence of any record itself indicate?
expectedAnswer: No - the absence of visible float consumption or critical-path impact in the schedule does not mean the suspension had no real effect; it most likely means the suspension was simply never recorded in the schedule at all, which is a data integrity and contemporaneous-updating failure, not evidence of zero impact. A genuine three-week stoppage should show up as either a calendar exception, a suspension/delay activity, or at minimum a visible gap between planned and actual progress dates for the affected activities during that window; its complete absence from the record suggests the update was not built contemporaneously from what actually happened on site.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate specifically recommends reconstructing the actual as-built sequence for the suspension period (from site diaries, correspondence, or the weather warning notices) and retroactively incorporating it into the schedule record, rather than accepting the five-week-later update's optimistic progress at face value.
expertAnswer: An expert flags this as a significant schedule-integrity and potential claims-preservation issue: if this suspension is not contemporaneously documented in the schedule, it becomes far harder to substantiate any later delay or disruption claim related to it, and the current schedule's apparent lack of impact could be misinterpreted (by the contractor itself, or in a later dispute) as evidence the event caused no delay, when in fact it is evidence of a broken update process. They would recommend an immediate corrective update reconstructing the suspension period and would treat this as a broader red flag about whether other periods have been similarly glossed over.
explanation: A schedule update that shows no impact from a known, real suspension event is not itself evidence the event was harmless - contemporaneous, accurate schedule updating is what allows real events to be reflected in Total Float, critical path, and forecast dates. Skipping the update during a suspension and then resuming as if nothing happened produces a schedule that no longer accurately represents what happened on site, undermining both its use as a management tool and its later evidentiary value for any delay or disruption claim.
reasoning: CPM schedules only reflect reality to the extent updates faithfully record actual start/finish dates, remaining durations, and any special conditions (like a suspension) as they occur. A five-week gap with no interim update and no record of the stoppage means the schedule engine had no data representing the suspension to calculate float consumption from - the absence of visible impact is a direct consequence of absent data, not proof of absent real-world impact.
commonMistakes: Concluding a known real-world event had no schedule impact simply because the current schedule shows none.
Not recognizing infrequent or skipped updates as a data integrity red flag in themselves.
Accepting a schedule update's smoothed-over progress without reconstructing what actually happened during a known gap.
redFlags: Candidate accepts the schedule's apparent lack of impact as proof the suspension did not matter.
Candidate does not flag the missed update cadence itself as a problem.

subcategory: Critical Path Drag vs Zero Float
skill: Explaining why shortening a zero-float critical activity does not always shorten the project by the same number of days
scenario: A river-crossing bridge project has two parallel critical paths reaching the same finish milestone: the bridge deck erection path (currently the longer of the two, driving the finish date, Total Float = 0) and the approach roadworks path (also Total Float = 0, running exactly the same length as the deck path after a recent update). The project team plans to compress deck erection by 10 days through additional shift work.
question: If deck erection is on the critical path with zero float, will shortening it by 10 days shorten the overall project finish by 10 days? Explain using the concept of 'critical path drag'.
expectedAnswer: No, not necessarily the full 10 days, and in this specific scenario, likely not at all beyond the point where the two paths are equal. Critical path 'drag' is the amount an activity's duration is actually adding to the overall project duration - for a genuinely sole critical path, drag typically equals the activity's duration (up to the point removing it would make another path critical). Here, because the approach roadworks path is already running exactly as long as the deck erection path (both currently Total Float = 0, i.e., both are co-critical), deck erection's true drag is limited: shortening it by 10 days will only shorten the project by the amount needed before the roadworks path becomes the new sole governing constraint, likely far less than the full 10 days, because once the deck path drops below the roadworks path's length, roadworks path becomes solely critical and further deck compression yields zero additional benefit to project finish.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly distinguishes float (schedule flexibility relative to a constraint) from drag (the activity's actual contribution to total project duration), and demonstrates the calculation: if both paths are currently exactly equal in length, shortening deck erection by even 1 day makes roadworks solely critical and governing, meaning deck erection's usable drag benefit toward the finish date is effectively at or near zero beyond that crossover point, even though deck erection remains 'critical' (zero float) throughout.
expertAnswer: An expert would recommend evaluating both paths together before committing resources to accelerate only the deck erection path, since spending money on shift work for deck erection alone, when a co-critical approach roadworks path exists, wastes the majority of the intended schedule benefit - genuine acceleration of the overall finish date requires compressing BOTH co-critical paths together (or the one that becomes solely governing after any change), a concept sometimes described as needing to attack the 'critical path set', not a single critical activity.
explanation: Total Float measures schedule flexibility relative to the current governing constraint and is a property of a whole path; it does not, by itself, tell you how much of the OVERALL project duration a specific activity is actually responsible for once other paths are considered. Critical path drag (a concept distinct from float) measures how much shortening an activity actually shortens the project, accounting for the fact that once a co-critical or near-critical parallel path becomes the new governing constraint, further compression of the original activity provides no additional benefit to the finish date, even though that activity remains, by definition, on a path with zero float.

So the true schedule benefit ('drag' reduction) of a 10-day deck erection compression is capped at whatever margin exists before the two paths cross, which could be much less than 10 days, or even zero if they are already exactly equal in length as stated.
